extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Euclid's Elements; teachers and scholars of classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, theorems and proof-construction norms for classical Euclidean circle-geometry (Book III): how to construct tangents/circles, prove equalities of arcs/angles, handle special cases and converses, and present constructions with logical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of tangents from an external point
rubrics_metrics.description: From a given external point two straight lines can be drawn to touch a given circle; these two tangents are equal in length and equally inclined to the line joining the external point to the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by joining the centre to the points of contact and proving the resulting triangles congruent (equal radii and equal sides). Explicitly note and treat the special case when the given point lies on the circumference (this case may be omitted by Euclid but is directly indicated by III.16 or by constructing the circle with the diameter through the point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent-radius perpendicularity (III.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line touches a circle and a radius is drawn to the point of contact, that radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by contradiction: assume another line from the centre to the tangent point is perpendicular, show side/angle comparisons (greater side subtends greater angle) lead to impossibility, and deduce uniqueness of the perpendicular radius. Cite prior basic results (e.g., I.17, I.19) in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse: perpendicular at contact passes through centre (III.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: If from the point of contact a straight line is drawn at right angles to the tangent, then that line passes through the centre of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove uniqueness by contradiction: suppose some other point is the centre and derive a contradiction comparing right angles. Emphasize that converses and partial converses should be stated and proved to clarify logical interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and prove partial converses / logical relations among properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When several related properties are present (tangent at a point, line from centre to contact, right angles at contact), state which pairs imply the third and provide partial converses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly enumerate combinations (e.g., (i)&(2) ⇒ (3); (i)&(3) ⇒ (2)) and give proofs or references so the reader can see equivalences and partial converses. This clarifies the logical structure of theorems and corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle at centre double angle at circumference (III.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a circle, the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference when both have the same circumference (arc) as base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use congruence / isosceles triangle arguments (radii equal) to show doubling. Treat separately cases where the angle at the centre is equal to or greater than two right angles (Euclid's text omits some of these cases; handle them explicitly if full generality is required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Angles in the same segment are equal (III.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Angles standing on the same arc (within the same segment) are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove using III.20 (angle-at-centre doubling). Note Euclid's proof as given only covers segments greater than a semicircle unless the 'angle at the centre' notion is extended; therefore explicitly handle the ≤ semicircle case separately (e.g., Simson's proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reductio ad absurdum for converses and existence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving converses (e.g., that a point must lie on a constructed circle) or impossibility statements, use contradiction arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show the circle through three points must also pass through a fourth vertex when vertical angles are equal, assume it does not and derive an impossible equality (e.g., exterior angle equals interior opposite). State the assumed opposite and the contradiction clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superposition/application to prove segment equality (III.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two similar segments on equal straight lines are equal, apply one segment to the other and reason about coincidence or impossibility of non-coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the method of applying a figure onto another (superposition) and exclude the three other placements (falls within, outside, or awry) by invoking geometric constraints (e.g., two circles cannot intersect in more than two points). Make the reference to the excluded possibility explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing the full circle from a given segment (III.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a segment of a circle, construct the complete circle of which it is a segment by locating the centre (perpendicular bisector of the chord) and drawing the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: bisect the chord at right angles, join endpoints, examine whether the centre falls inside, on, or outside the segment by comparing angles (angle ABD vs angle BAD), and construct accordingly. Explicitly state after construction that the circle with the found centre and radius passes through the remaining points of the segment so that the constructed circle actually coincides with the given segment; consider cases (segment <, =, or > semicircle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly handle special and singular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and either include or justify omission of special cases (e.g., given point lying on circumference, chord passing through centre, arc equal to a semicircle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid sometimes omits trivial or directly indicated cases; when presenting or evaluating a proof, either include these cases or state clearly why they are omitted and how they follow from earlier propositions (e.g., by III.16 or straightforward application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and reuse of prior propositions (citation practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should cite previously established results (e.g., I.4, I.17, III.16, III.20) to justify steps rather than re-proving elementary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking earlier results, give proposition numbers and briefly state which part is being used (e.g., SAS, angle-in-semicircle, equality of radii). This keeps proofs concise and traceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use triangle-congruence (SAS/isosceles) to prove equal sides/angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish equalities of sides or angles by constructing triangles and proving them congruent via equal sides and included angles (often using radii or perpendicular bisectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical patterns: equal radii → isosceles triangles → equal base angles; equal sides plus right angles → equal bases (I.4). Make the congruence pattern explicit in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral sum to two right angles; converses (III.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, opposite angles add to two right angles; conversely, if opposite angles sum to two right angles a circumcircle can be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove using angles-in-same-segment (III.21) and triangle-angle-sum. For the converse provide a construction for the circumcircle (III.9 or IV.5) and prove by reductio that the circle must pass through the fourth vertex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal circles: equal angles stand on equal circumferences and converses (III.26–27)
rubrics_metrics.description: In equal circles equal central or inscribed angles subtend equal arcs (circumferences), and conversely equal arcs imply equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove forward direction by equality of radii and SAS to get equal chord lengths; reduce special angle-size cases (right or obtuse) using III.30/31 or subdividing angles. For converses use contradiction: construct an equal angle on one circle and show arc-length inequalities are impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences (III.28–29)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal chords in equal circles (or same circle) cut off equal greater and lesser arcs; conversely equal arcs determine equal chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centres, equal radii and equal included central angles (III.26–27) leading to equal arcs; handle the particular/degenerate cases (chord through centre = diameter) explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisect a circumference (III.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: To bisect a given arc, bisect the chord and erect the perpendicular through the midpoint to the chord; the intersection with the arc bisects the circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate equality of resulting arcs by showing the corresponding chords are equal (congruence) and use earlier results that equal chords cut equal arcs. Explicitly check that resulting arcs are each less than a semicircle if required by preceding propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle-in-semicircle and segment-angle inequalities (III.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle in a semicircle is right; the angle in a greater segment is less than a right angle and the angle in a less segment greater than a right angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by isosceles/radius arguments and triangle-angle-sum; treat cases where the 'angle at the centre' might be ≥ two right angles separately. Note alternative historical proofs exist; if invoking corollaries, verify they are not later interpolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit fundamental geometric constraints as proof tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use invariant constraints (e.g., two circles cannot intersect in more than two points; diameter is greatest chord) to exclude impossible configurations and complete arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using such constraints, state them explicitly and show how a hypothesized configuration would violate them (e.g., would create >2 intersections), producing the contradiction needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in hypothesis → inference mapping and scope of inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple hypotheses are present, make clear which inference follows from which hypothesis and avoid ambiguous attribution (e.g., which hypothesis yields the conclusion about intersection behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer punctuation or phrasing that ties inferences to the correct hypothesis; when multiple cases are considered, label them and indicate which lines of argument dispose of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Porisms/Corollaries and explicit completion statements
rubrics_metrics.description: After constructive proofs, explicitly state porisms/corollaries or that the constructed object indeed satisfies the required condition (e.g., the circle drawn with centre E and radius AE passes through the remaining segment points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if 'obvious', explicitly record the finishing statement so readers understand the intended coincidence/equality; be cautious about including later interpolated corollaries without justification.
